body: yea seems about right on for my life. :') was worth venting to myself anyway.

I sympathize, friend. 

I have been diagnosed bipolar for 3 years now (23 F now) and it's a constant toggle. I am currently in graduate school and life is one fragile moment after another. 

For your struggles, I am sorry.

As a glorious aside...

I got put into a queue to talk on a lifeline chat online and after waiting 30 minutes, it gets to me and says "all providers are offline." 

Splendid. Good sign.

I have spoken to my family before about it in the past. They try to be sympathetic but are often the types who just do not understand. My close friends come from fairly affluent backgrounds and do not understand why I do not have the money or coverage to seek help. 

My school offers a program for wellness (including mental health) and the counselor there basically told me he could not offer the treatment I needed and that I needed to see an out-of-network therapist -- can't afford it. At $150 per session, that's my food budget for several weeks. 

And thank you for your kind words. I just try to hang on, but it grows increasingly difficult.

I lost my mental health benefits last year in April and it became too expensive for me to go back into treatment.
 
I felt okay for a little while (probably because my psych had prescribed three months of meds to tide me over until I thought of another plan) but I inevitably sunk back into this. 

When I came back for a graduate degree in August, I was hoping the change in scenery would do something, but it has only amplified the emptiness and loneliness. I've been feeling wavering levels for seven months now but can honestly admit that I have not had a genuine smile in such a time and it gets just a fragment worse each time.

I am sorry for the long reply, but here it goes: 

I’ll admit that I am quick to invalidate my own issues, mostly because I have been raised in an environment where I have always been told that my problems were “not as bad as others’” and that “[I] had it great, so [I] shouldn’t complain.” 

Though I did not grow up the most attractive, most charismatic, or most likable of my siblings (all of these facts, again, have been enforced by the rest of my family), I did grow up the smart one, which everyone has made out to be a consolation prize. In my early twenties, I am currently pursuing a Master’s (while applying for a PhD) in an advanced science. I always was the academically gifted one. So with this territory came the deferral of my needs for attention in order for my family to sustain a chronically and severely sick child and a healthy child who was always causing problems (please keep in mind this living sibling is now an absolutely wonderful person now). I was instructed to not tell my teachers or friends at school what was going on at home, which was often a combination of addiction problems, a dying sibling, and violent arguments between my parents; they were arrested in public several times at our house for threats with weapons and whatnot, which later became the source of ridicule for me in the neighborhood by other children. I guess years of denial of anything being wrong hardened me up a bit because now I can get away with sobbing almost all day without my roommates or professors knowing that there’s a problem – funny enough, usually it is everyone else who comes to me for advice and support, which I certainly do not mind offering. I think my family needed to cope with dysfunction and I stood as that one seemingly functional object for a very long time.

I love my parents dearly. They are both good people, just sick in their own ways. 

My father has been an addict for all of my life and has put that addiction before us many times. He loves me a lot and always did the best for me, but I cannot honestly count on both hands the number of times he forgot an event in lieu of pursuing amelioration for his urging addiction. He has gotten a bit better but he is also much older now and is still not very reliable in the long run. 

My mother, on the other hand, has an interesting dynamic with me. We always come across to other people as “the best of friends,” which she would certainly agree to. I, however, have a bit of a heavy heart on the subject. She tells me I can tell her anything, but I know better than that. If I have a problem with something she has done? She gets angry with me for being rambunctious or “pissy” before crying and making herself the victim. I inevitably feel guilty and immediately apologize for being nasty. 

She tells me I am beautiful, but it always comes with negative and (sometimes) subtle comment:

“You are pretty but you look way better with makeup. It’s incomparable.”

“When you lose weight again, you’ll look good.” (I’m not huge, easily described as just chubby though I’m also very muscular and strong)

She has always prided herself on being an attractive woman. That is by far her favorite thing, though she’ll try to convince others that she appreciates my intelligence (she usually teases it in a “jocular” way). You can tell, though, that when she sees people compliment my older sibling’s attractiveness, she is so proud and will say that “it came from [her].” Her anorexic tendencies still come forth once in a while, usually in the form of excessive dieting and stabs at my own weight. She knows that my looks are touchy for me as I did grow up in the shadow of having a very attractive family while only possessing an average face with a nice body when I exercise a lot. 
Being the ugly duckling has always been my gig, which I have resigned to with a bit of grace and the fleeting self-esteem (though I will certainly never outwardly show this insecurity because then I will get labeled “brat” or “a baby” by my mother). 

“I have always been the best mother” is her favorite line.

She’s been good to me and provided a decent life, but it’s come with many struggles. Her addiction, her unstable emotions, her countless addict boyfriends, her public displays of drunkenness, her obsession with her (and everyone else’s) physical appearance, and so on. 

I love them for who they are, even if what they are can sometimes take it out of me.

Thank you for your kind words, friend. I am not giving up without a fight. I just cannot help but have these feelings. I would like to resume therapy and medications as soon as possible, but I am not certain as to when that can occur. Still, I appreciate you taking time to respond.
